editor_note: Guided tour of a listed Victorian building with archive material, a secret chapel and rooftop views over East London.

listing.blurb: A guided tour of the Grade II listed building that houses Oxford House, the Bethnal Green community arts centre that began in 1884 as the original settlement house. One for local history fans.

story.then: Oxford House's own history page says volunteers from Keble College lived there and gave practical support to people in East London, including labour exchanges, adult classes, clubs and legal advice. In the Second World War the building sheltered up to 300 neighbours and evacuated local children to boarding schools. After a major refurbishment in 2019 it has a theatre of 120 seats, plus a gallery, dance studio, Victorian chapel, cafe and roof terrace.
story.now: The tour is part of Made in the East End, a two-year heritage project with National Lottery money behind it. According to the venue's own website, it covers the building's role in both world wars, key pieces from an archive reaching back to the Victorian period, and Gandhi's visit in the 1930s, the venue's most famous visitor.
worth_knowing: The building came through the war without damage, though about 80 tons of bombs fell on East London.
At its peak, more than 1,000 people were on the membership waiting list.
Princess Anne visited in 1984 for the celebrations marking Oxford House's centenary.
The rooftop is reached by a spiral staircase of 24 steps.

evidence.quote: Oxford House has been based in Bethnal Green since 1884.
volunteers from Keble College lived at Oxford House and provided practical support to the community of East London.
Schemes to tackle the challenges of urban poverty included legal advice, youth and working men’s clubs, labour exchanges, and adult education courses.
During World War II, Oxford House evacuated local children to free boarding schools, while at home the building served as a bomb shelter for up to 300 community members
we underwent a major refurbishment in 2019 and are now home to a 120-seat theatre, gallery, dance studio, Victorian chapel, café and roof terrace.
Made in the East End is an inspiring heritage 2-years project funded by The National Lottery Heritage Fund
Hear about the role our building played in World War I and World War II.
Take a look at key pieces in our Archive which dates back to the Victorian period.
Learn more about Oxford House’s most famous visitor – Gandhi in the 1930s.
Oxford House was fortunate to avoid damage during the war when 80 tons of bombs were dropped on East London.
the waiting list for membership stood at over 1000 people at its peak!
To celebrate the centenary of Oxford House in 1984, Princess Anne made a visit for the celebratory events.
access to our rooftop is via spiral staircase with 24 steps.
